title: The Collar Bomb Heist
summary: True crime episode on the 2003 Erie, Pennsylvania collar bomb heist. Pizza delivery driver Brian Wells walked into a PNC bank wearing a homemade collar bomb and demanded $250,000, then was caught in a parking lot and died when the bomb detonated. Hosts cover the scavenger hunt notes left for him, the investigation that led to Bill Rothstein's dead body and the confession of Marjorie Deal Armstrong, Armstrong's prior murder conviction, informant Kenneth Barnes's testimony at her trial, her conviction as mastermind, and the unresolved questions about Wells's complicity. The episode ends with listener mail about John Adams's sun drawings in his diary.

segments.title: Opening banter and true crime preview
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the true crime episode, describing a heist involving a bomb, a scavenger hunt, a crack dealer and prostitutes, and joke about the Geo Metro pizza car.

segments.title: The bank robbery and collar bomb
segments.summary: Brian Wells, a pizza delivery driver in Erie, Pennsylvania, leaves a pizza run around 2 pm in August 2003 and walks into a PNC bank wearing a collar bomb and demanding $250,000 with a note. He leaves, is found by state troopers in a nearby parking lot, and the bomb detonates after about 25 minutes, killing him. The bomb's construction and the scavenger hunt notes are described.

segments.title: Scavenger hunt and early investigation
segments.summary: Wells had reached the first note at a McDonald's; police followed the hunt to a jar where the next note was missing. The case went cold, and investigators examined the pizza delivery location. A reporter for the Erie Times News visited neighbor Bill Rothstein, who was not further questioned by police.

segments.title: Rothstein's body and Marjorie Deal Armstrong's arrest
segments.summary: Months later Bill Rothstein called 911 and revealed a body in his freezer, the ex-boyfriend of his former girlfriend Marjorie Deal Armstrong, whom he helped cover up. He worried about her, and police arrested her. She pled guilty but mentally ill to the Jim Roden killing and was sentenced to seven to twenty years. Rothstein died of cancer in 2004.

segments.title: Armstrong's confession and informants
segments.summary: Informants in jail said Armstrong was the mastermind. She admitted involvement, providing kitchen timers and being nearby, and toured police around Erie. Kenneth Barnes, a crack dealer, was recruited by her brother-in-law and became a witness against her in exchange for a reduced sentence.

segments.title: Trial, motive and conviction
segments.summary: Armstrong's competency to stand trial was questioned, and she was diagnosed with cancer. The indictment named Rothstein and Wells as conspirators, which Wells's family disputed. Barnes testified that Armstrong wanted her father killed and funded it through the heist, and that Wells was tied to crack debts and forced into the device. Armstrong testified she never met Wells. The jury convicted her of armed bank robbery, conspiracy and use of a destructive device; she died in prison about seven years later.

segments.title: Unresolved questions and accomplices
segments.summary: Retired FBI investigator Jim Fisher argues Rothstein was the true mastermind. Floyd Stockton, who allegedly helped with the collar bomb, received immunity. The hosts discuss whether Wells was complicit.

segments.title: Listener mail: John Adams emoji
segments.summary: A listener shares that John Adams's diary entries from 1756 included small sun drawings as an early emoji-like habit, and mentions a Boston history podcast.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and contact information and sign off.
